prompt: Which of these reagents cleaves most ethers?

choices.why: Halogens have no effect on most ethers.
Dilute acids have no effect on most ethers; cleavage needs a strong acid such as HBr or HI.
Bases have no effect on most ethers.

explanation: Ethers are unreactive toward halogens, dilute acids, bases, and nucleophiles, which is why they are widely used as reaction solvents. Their only truly general reaction is cleavage by strong acids such as aqueous HBr and HI.

prompt: Which of these acids does NOT cleave ethers?

choices.why: Aqueous HBr works well; ethyl phenyl ether gives phenol and bromoethane, for example.
Aqueous HI works well; ethyl isopropyl ether gives isopropyl alcohol and iodoethane, for example.
Trifluoroacetic acid cleaves tert-butyl ethers by an E1 mechanism, even at 0 °C.

explanation: Aqueous HBr and HI both cleave ethers well, but HCl does not. Ethers with a tertiary group are a special case; tert-butyl ethers cleave even with trifluoroacetic acid at 0 °C.

prompt: What products form when ethyl phenyl ether, C6H5OCH2CH3, is heated with aqueous HBr?

choices.why: The bond from oxygen to the ring stays intact; bromide ion ends up on the ethyl group.
HBr cleavage gives one alkyl bromide along with the phenol, not two compounds with –OH groups.

choices.text: No reaction, because ethers are inert to acids
choices.why: Strong acids such as aqueous HBr do cleave ethers.

explanation: Ethers undergo one truly general reaction: cleavage by strong acids. The section's first example shows ethyl phenyl ether heated with aqueous HBr to give phenol and bromoethane.

prompt: Ethyl isopropyl ether, CH3CH2OCH(CH3)2, is cleaved by HI. What are the products?

choices.why: Iodide attacks the less hindered primary carbon, not the more hindered secondary one.
An ether with only primary and secondary groups reacts by S_N2, not by E1.
S_N2 cleavage breaks only one C–O bond, giving a single alcohol and a single alkyl halide.

explanation: Ethers with only primary and secondary alkyl groups react by an S_N2 mechanism, with I− attacking the protonated ether at the less hindered site. Ethyl isopropyl ether exclusively yields isopropyl alcohol and iodoethane, because iodide attacks the primary ethyl carbon.

prompt: What are the products when sec-butyl methyl ether, CH3OCH(CH3)CH2CH3, is cleaved with HI?

choices.why: That would need attack at the more hindered secondary carbon. With only methyl and secondary groups, iodide attacks the less hindered methyl carbon.
An E1 cleavage needs a tertiary, benzylic, or allylic group. This ether has only methyl and secondary groups, so it reacts by S_N2.
S_N2 cleavage breaks one C–O bond, giving a single alkyl halide and a single alcohol.

explanation: With no tertiary, benzylic, or allylic group, cleavage is S_N2 at the less hindered site. The methyl carbon is less hindered than the secondary carbon, so I− attacks it, giving iodomethane and 2-butanol.

prompt: Which of these ethers would cleave in acid by an S_N1 or E1 mechanism rather than by S_N2?

choices.why: Both groups are primary, so diethyl ether cleaves by S_N2.
Its groups are primary and secondary, so it cleaves by S_N2 at the ethyl carbon.
Both groups are primary, so dipropyl ether cleaves by S_N2.

explanation: Ethers with a tertiary, benzylic, or allylic group cleave by an S_N1 or E1 mechanism. Ethers with only primary and secondary alkyl groups react by S_N2. Of these four, only tert-butyl methyl ether has a tertiary group.

prompt: Why do ethers with a tertiary, benzylic, or allylic group cleave by S_N1 or E1 mechanisms?

choices.text: These groups can form stable carbocation intermediates
These groups are the least hindered sites for nucleophilic attack
choices.why: Tertiary groups are the most hindered. Their advantage is that they form stable carbocations.

choices.text: These groups prevent the ether oxygen from being protonated
choices.why: The oxygen is still protonated; then the C–O bond breaks to give a stable carbocation.

choices.text: These groups make the C–O bond stronger and harder to break
choices.why: The C–O bond breaks easily here, because the carbocation that forms is stable.

explanation: Tertiary, benzylic, and allylic substrates can produce stable intermediate carbocations, so their ethers cleave by S_N1 or E1 mechanisms. These reactions are often fast and take place at moderate temperatures.

prompt: What are the main products when tert-butyl propyl ether, (CH3)3COCH2CH2CH3, reacts with HBr?

choices.why: Attack at the less hindered carbon is the rule only when both groups are primary or secondary. With a tertiary group, the tertiary C–O bond breaks by S_N1.
Only the tertiary C–O bond breaks; the propyl group stays on oxygen and ends up as 1-propanol.

choices.text: No reaction, because ethers resist acids
choices.why: Strong acids such as HBr cleave ethers, and ethers with a tertiary group react especially easily.

explanation: One group is tertiary and one is primary. An ether with a tertiary alkyl group usually cleaves by an S_N1 mechanism at the tertiary C–O bond, giving 2-bromo-2-methylpropane and 1-propanol; a competing E1 reaction might also give some alkene (Worked Example 18.3.1).

prompt: What are the products when tert-butyl cyclohexyl ether is treated with trifluoroacetic acid at 0 °C?

choices.why: The tert-butyl group, not the secondary cyclohexyl group, forms the stable carbocation, so cyclohexanol is released.
The reaction is E1: the tert-butyl cation loses a proton and ends up as the alkene 2-methylpropene.

choices.text: No reaction, because ether cleavage needs heating
choices.why: Ethers with a tertiary group often cleave fast at moderate temperatures; this one reacts at 0 °C.

explanation: tert-Butyl ethers react by an E1 mechanism on treatment with trifluoroacetic acid at 0 °C. tert-Butyl cyclohexyl ether gives cyclohexanol (90%) and 2-methylpropene. This reaction is often used in the laboratory synthesis of peptides.

prompt: Which mechanism describes the acid-induced cleavage of tert-butyl cyclohexyl ether to cyclohexanol and 2-methylpropene?

choices.text: Protonation of the ether oxygen, followed by an E1 reaction
S_N2 attack of trifluoroacetate ion on the cyclohexyl carbon
choices.why: The cyclohexyl C–O bond stays intact, since cyclohexanol is a product. The tert-butyl group is the one that leaves.

choices.text: A one-step E2 reaction in which a base removes a proton as the C–O bond breaks
choices.why: The reaction runs in acid and goes through a tertiary carbocation, so it is E1, not E2.

choices.text: Protonation of the ether oxygen, followed by S_N2 attack at the tertiary carbon
choices.why: Tertiary carbons don't undergo S_N2 reactions; the tertiary group leaves as a carbocation.

explanation: The acid protonates the ether oxygen. The protonated ether then loses the tert-butyl group as a stable tertiary carbocation, which loses a proton to give 2-methylpropene, leaving cyclohexanol. This is an E1 reaction (Exercise 18.3.2).
